extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in media studies, journalism scholars, and advanced journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative dimensions for content analysis of mass media (television, news, magazines), focusing on representation by race, gender, age, occupation, geography, and power relations. Includes methodological benchmarks (comparisons with demographic/geographic data) and interpretive criteria (stereotyping, symbolic annihilation, agenda-setting).

rubrics_metrics.name: portrayal of professions and gender-role stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: "doctors, among the most frequently portrayed professionals, are treated as 'demigods,' whereas nurses are seen as subservient to doctors and sometimes as sex objects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how occupations are gendered and sexualized; check for recurring tropes (male professionals/authority vs. female subservients) and specific examples (male doctor/female nurse, male lawyer/female secretary). Note overrepresentation of professionals/managers as indicators of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: ethnic representation and under-representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "the model prime-time television character is a white male... Minorities are under-represented across the world of prime time" (Greenberg, Signorielli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the proportion of racial/ethnic groups among characters and compare with population benchmarks; flag low speaking-role percentages (e.g., Hispanics 1.5% of speaking characters vs. ~9% population in Greenberg's study) and concentration of minorities in limited program types.

rubrics_metrics.name: ethnic stereotyping (content and tropes)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a stereotype is an oversimplified picture... These ethnic stereotypes have given rise to many inaccurate and disparaging media portrayals of American Indians (primitive and savage), Asians (Fu Manchu: corrupt and violent), Latinos (hot-tempered and lazy), and African Americans (shiftless and easily frightened)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring stereotypical characterizations and tropes for specific ethnic groups; document language, imagery, and recurring narrative roles that convey such simplifications; note contextual causes (appealing to majority audiences) and examples (editorial cartoons, slurs).

rubrics_metrics.name: event-driven stereotyping and opportunistic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: coverage of the 50th anniversary of Pearl Harbor and Japan received "much of which had racist overtones" (Quigley, 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage around anniversaries/crises amplifies stereotypes or racist framing; analyze how contemporary political/economic contexts (e.g., Japan's economic position) shape evaluative language and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: roles, status, and typecasting of African-American characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Blacks "tend to play more minor roles in less prestigious occupations, be more often victimized by crime, and be more involved in crime and killing... Half of these African-American characters are concentrated in a few comedy series... more likely to be stereotyped and of a lower socioeconomic status."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code role prominence, occupational prestige, socioeconomic indicators, and involvement in crime/victimization for black characters; note concentration in program genres and age distributions (many under age 20).

rubrics_metrics.name: comparative benchmarks: demographic and geographic representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Implicit in such studies... is that news and entertainment programming should represent the world in amounts proportionate to population, land mass, ethnic distribution, or some other criterion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external standards (census demographics, geographic distribution) to compare media content proportions; but include caveat that news/drama select salient events and not a literal "slice of life." Explicitly state benchmark(s) used and justify limits of direct comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender representation and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: "Women are outnumbered three to one, they are young, and overrepresented in lower level jobs, situation comedies, and family dramas... Women are vastly outnumbered by men, are younger than men, and are featured in traditional, stereotyped roles... women are more likely than males to be depicted as victims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate numerical representation, age distribution, occupational status, and narrative roles of women; look for language that marks gender (e.g., 'female candidate' vs no label for white male); document stereotyped portrayals across media types (TV, news, magazines, commercials).

rubrics_metrics.name: age distribution and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: "People 20 to 49 years of age represented two-thirds of television characters, but only one-third of the census population... both very young and very old are underrepresented and negatively stereotyped on television."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare on-screen age groups with population proportions; identify whether older people (especially older women) and children are underrepresented or portrayed negatively; analyze age-by-gender interactions (older men treated more favorably than older women).

rubrics_metrics.name: violence, victimization, and power relations in portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gerbner has viewed violence as a shorthand way of expressing power: Who has the power to victimize... White males are the most likely victimizers, whereas old, young, and minority women are the most likely victims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code perpetrators vs victims by demographic categories; interpret violence as symbolic expression of power—who is shown as agentive vs powerless; consider frequency and context of antisocial acts by gender and race.

rubrics_metrics.name: magazine fiction portrayals of women
rubrics_metrics.description: "all the women in fiction stories were defined by the absence or presence of men in their lives... work for women was treated as secondary to their home life... heroines tended to be young and attractive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In magazine fiction and features, analyze whether female characters are defined relationally (by men), whether employment is marginalized, and look for repeated emphasis on youth and attractiveness; include sample outlets (Ladies Home Journal, Good Housekeeping) as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: political coverage bias toward female candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: "female candidates get less coverage than their male counterparts, but the women's coverage was more about their viability as candidates (shown as low) and less about their stands on issues."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure quantity and quality of political coverage by candidate gender; code whether coverage focuses on electability/viability/personality vs policy positions; document differences in framing and topic allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: source selection and elite bias
rubrics_metrics.description: "News media reflect these power relations in the selection of sources, by relying on officials and other wealthy, corporate, and bureaucratic elites. These people are covered routinely. Less powerful people... gain news attention when they become extremists... often evaluated through establishment sources."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who is quoted/used as sources (officials, corporate elites, grassroots actors), frequency by source type, and whether less powerful actors are framed as deviant or mediated through elite interpretation. Consider stationing of bureaus and proximity to power centers as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: geographic and international coverage bias
rubrics_metrics.description: "Which states are mentioned most often? Those on the East and West Coasts... Internationally, which are the most powerful countries? The Western world and its adversaries... The Third World is less powerful, matters less... heard from only when a great calamity breaks through the news threshold."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess geographic concentration of coverage (states, cities, countries) relative to importance/power; code topics/events that trigger Third World coverage versus routine coverage of powerful countries; note bureau placement as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: media consonance, convergence, and diversity of voices
rubrics_metrics.description: "there is a great deal of commonality among content presented by the various media, what has been called 'media consonance'... When the media 'converge' around a few key sources and certain issues, the result is that the media have more power to influence the audience—there are fewer 'voices' and hence less diversity in media content."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure overlap/convergence across outlets in sources, frames, and issue selection; evaluate number of distinct voices represented and the extent to which dominant media set the agenda for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: symbolic annihilation (minimization through under- or misrepresentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In Gaye Tuchman's terms, the media have the ability to express lack of power by minimizing people through 'symbolic annihilation,' by under- or misrepresenting them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify omissions, marginalization, or distorted portrayals of groups (race, gender, class, age); document presence/absence and quality of representation rather than only counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: news selection for impact/newsworthiness vs 'slice of life'
rubrics_metrics.description: "We depend on news to alert us to things that aren't going well... It's more efficient for news to alert us to things that have an impact on our lives than those that don't... both drama and news single out some features of the environment and emphasize them over others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating coverage, account for normative criteria of newsworthiness (impact, deviation, proximity) that make direct proportional representation unrealistic; code selection criteria explicitly (impact, timeliness, conflict) and distinguish normative selection from biased omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: methodological benchmarks for content studies (comparisons and longitudinal changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: "some [studies] have explicitly compared media patterns with demographic, geographic, and other external benchmarks. Other studies compare changes in media coverage of an issue over time... For much content, though, there can be no easy way to calibrate it in relation to other standards."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both cross-sectional benchmark comparisons (demographic/geographic) and longitudinal analyses to detect trends; state limitations and justify chosen benchmarks; where direct calibration is impossible, use relative or thematic measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: treatment of nontraditional/minority groups (LGBTQ, elderly, immigrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: increasing acceptance of personal classified ads for homosexuals with editorial inspection; immigrant reliance on media images in forming impressions of the U.S.; elderly are "disproportionately low" in coverage though not necessarily stereotyped negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code presence and framing of LGBTQ people, immigrants, and elderly across media types; evaluate whether representations are stigmatizing, tokenistic, absent, or substantive; include policies (e.g., ad inspection) and audience effects (immigrants using media to form impressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: interpretive principle: media content as both a manifestation and source of culture
rubrics_metrics.description: "media content is both that and a source of culture. That is, media content takes elements of culture, magnifies them, frames them, and feeds them back to an audience... media content may serve as either a catalyst for or a brake on this change."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, include interpretive assessment of how media magnify, reinforce, or challenge cultural norms; evaluate potential societal implications (reinforcement of stereotypes, impediment to change) in addition to descriptive measures.
